articles.title: England vs Pakistan: 'Chickens come home to roost' for PCB as 'dismal' batting sees tourists bowled out within 34 overs in final Test
articles.summary: Pakistan's crisis-hit series against England worsened on day one of the third Test when they were bowled out for 133 within 34 overs; the third Test between England and Pakistan, at Edgbaston, continues live on Sky Sports on Thursday, September 10
articles.body:
"Unprecedented" was the word used by Sky Sports Cricket's Michael Atherton to describe the upheaval that has occurred over the last week in response to heavy losses at Headingley and Lords.

Seven players were sent home, head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul were replaced, and an investigation began into "media reports concerning discipline and conduct".

If those actions were aimed at provoking a response, the Pakistan Cricket Board did not get the one it would have been after on day one at Edgbaston.

On the eve of the third Test, Root dismissed suggestions that Pakistan have shown "no fight" in the series as disrespectful to both teams.

But after four hours of day one Josh Tongue (4-42), Ollie Robinson (3-15), and Jofra Archer (3-25) had cleaned them up with relative ease.

By over 10, Pakistan were four down with just 29 runs on the board. It took England 11 more overs to take three more wickets, Pakistan posting just 71 more runs by lunch with a dismal 110-7 on the board.

Things were wrapped up by the 34th over, a total of 133 all the visitors could muster on what was described in the Sky Sports commentary box as a "blameless" pitch. It has been a low-scoring summer, but this was low even by those standards.

But was any other outcome expected? Or was the display delivered actually the most likely amid an extremely testing set of circumstances.

"A thoroughly miserable batting performance from them," said Atherton.

"It is a batting line-up woefully low on confidence, " he later added.

"The decision to send seven players home - the chickens are coming home to roost. You cannot treat players like that and expect to build confidence in a side.

"Everybody who plays professional sport knows that if you play badly, the axe is going to fall.

"For all the criticism that has been made, just bear the context in mind that this Pakistan team looks dispirited - and there is a reason for that."

Pakistan's issues have been laid bare, and it is not going to be a quick fix. If they lose this, they will have one victory in their last seven Tests.

Couple that with the clear unrest and more upheaval seems almost inevitable.

"When I saw what happened, you could almost not see where the inspiration would come from - with the skill, the experience, and the alien conditions," said Sky Sports Cricket's Urooj Mumtaz.

"But to top all of it, the turbulent conditions and the manner in which [the changes were made to the side].

"Underwhelming, absolutely no competition, and this is the worst we've seen so far."

'Impossible' to play good cricket with off-field turmoil

So was it too big an ask of Pakistan to even muster up a semblance of fight?

Sky Sports Cricket's Stuart Broad said: "It looks like a really difficult environment to play in.

"You often talk about playing with freedom, playing without fear but the worst place you can be is feeling you need 20 or 30 runs to stay in the team - you never warm together as a group.

"It's really impossible to play good cricket when you have that many off-field problems going."

Pakistan find solace in debutant Razaullah

England ended day one with a narrow lead of 23 runs after losing four wickets. Two of them came from "bright spark" Razaullah (2-42), who provided Pakistan with some hope on his debut.

The 21-year-old hit speeds of over 90mph and took the key wicket of Joe Root to reinvigorate his team and show that the future of Pakistan cricket still has potential.

On day two, it will be about whether the youngster can continue his strong showing with ball in hand to make his side's poor batting performance count for as little as possible.

"Pakistan have been calling out for something different from their bowlers for a long while," said Sky Sports Cricket's Nasser Hussain.

"It is nice to watch that spell from Razaullah that had something, that had a point of difference, had some pace.

"It hurried one of the greatest batters there has ever been in Joe Root, and got him out."

Second Test (Lord's) - England won by 194 runs

articles.title: Big boost for India ahead of Afghanistan T20Is as Nitish Kumar Reddy clears fitness test
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: All-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy has received the green signal from the BCCI medical staff and is set to join the rest of the India squad in .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: All-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy has received the green signal from the BCCI medical staff and is set to join the rest of the India squad in the national capital on Thursday ahead of the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan, starting on September 13, the TimesofIndia.com can confirm.Reddy last played for India in the ODI series against Afghanistan earlier this year in June, where he aggravated his left quadriceps injury. The 23-year-old had initially sustained the injury while bowling in the first ODI in Dharamsala and was subsequently rested for the second match in Lucknow. Reddy returned for the third ODI in Chennai, where he experienced discomfort again. He then missed India's recent white-ball tours of Ireland and England because of the injury.It is learnt that Reddy passed his fitness test last week, following which he was picked for the Afghanistan series. On Wednesday, he underwent a final match simulation at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru, which he passed in flying colours. It also is understood that he is bowling workload ticked all boxes and he seems ready for even the longer grind.Reddy is also part of India's squad for the Asian Games, which begin on September 24. India won the men's gold medal at the previous edition of the Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, in October 2023. They were adjudged winners on the basis of being the higher-seeded team in the final against Afghanistan after the match was washed out.Indian team will depart for Asian Games from Delhi on September 18. Before the start of the Asian Games, Team India will also play a solitary T20I against Japan n September 22 at the Sano International Cricket Ground in Tochigi PrefectureIndia men's T20I squad for Asian Games: Shreyas Iyer (capt), Sanju Samson (wk), Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan (wk), Shivam Dube, Tilak Varma (vice-capt), Axar Patel, Washington Sundar, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Varun Chakravarthy, Ravi Bishnoi, Harshit Rana, Arshdeep Singh, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Jasprit Bumrah.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Crowd gathers outside hotel containing Pakistan under-19 cricket team
articles.summary: People gather at a hotel as Pakistan's under-16 cricket team are wrongly identified as migrants.
articles.body:
An international cricket team became the mistaken focus of an anti-migrant protest after being spotted entering a hotel in Portsmouth.

Reform county councillor George Madgwick said about 30 to 40 people gathered outside the Marriott Hotel in Cosham on Tuesday evening, amid false rumours that a group of migrants had arrived by bus.

In a Facebook post, he urged people not to attend, saying hotel staff showed him "proof" the guests were the touring Pakistan under-19 national cricket team.

Hampshire Constabulary confirmed officers responded to reports of a gathering outside the hotel shortly before 18:30 BST.

A police spokesperson said officers spoke to the people "who were expressing concerns about a coach that had been seen in the area".

"The officers explained that their concerns were not correct," they said, adding: "No offences were identified."

The crowd of about 30 people left shortly before 21:00, the spokesperson said.

In his Facebook post, Madgwick said: "I visited the manager and the hotel explained it was the Pakistani cricket team staying.

"The cricket team coach came to speak to me personally and I saw proof (hotel were happy to provide)."

Speaking to the BBC, he said: "Someone online saw a group of what looked like foreign nationals leaving the coach and put a photo of it online and that's where it spurred from.

"It was mere speculation rather than based on truth or fact.

"In this case they have made a grave error, a grave mistake."

Responding to criticism and comments on his Facebook post, Madgwick denied the reaction to the cricketers' arrival had been racist.

He said: "I think one person made the assumption and everybody else followed that assumption.

"It isn't a good reflection on our city.

"It's not something I want our city to be known for."

The incident happened two days after hundreds of protesters blocked roads in the city after a boat carrying about 120 migrants was brought ashore.

Amanda Martin, Labour MP for Portsmouth North, called the hotel incident "deeply concerning".

She said: "It's completely unacceptable that misinformation has led to young cricketers visiting our city being wrongly targeted and mistaken for people seeking asylum.

"It's also wrong that people who work in the hotels had to deal with this.

"Those who arrived in Portsmouth on Sunday were transported outside of Hampshire for processing.

"There is a legitimate debate to be had about immigration, but it must be based on facts not misinformation or rumour."

The BBC understands the England and Wales Cricket Board has checked on wellbeing of the Pakistani under-19s team, and is reviewing security arrangements for the remainder of their tour.

The Marriott Hotel Portsmouth has declined to comment.

articles.title: Harshit Rana likely to miss Afghanistan T20Is; Asian Games in danger too
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Harshit Rana’s return to international cricket will take some more time as the speedster has injured himself during the match simulation, w.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Harshit Rana’s return to international cricket will take some more time as the speedster has injured himself during the match simulation, which was part of the Return to Play (RTP) protocol, on Tuesday. It is understood that the injury does not look good at the moment and has put a major question mark over his participation in both the Afghanistan T20Is and the upcoming Asian Games.Harshit Rana sustained a hamstring injury in the third T20I against England at Trent Bridge earlier this year.Rana injured his knee during India's warm-up match against South Africa in the lead-up to the 2026 Men's T20 World Cup and was subsequently ruled out of that tournament. He then underwent surgery and missed the Indian Premier League (IPL) 2026 as well while playing for Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR).After completing his rehabilitation, Rana was added to the India squad for the third ODI against Afghanistan in Chennai on June 20.As TOI.com reported earlier, Nitish Kumar Reddy has received the all-clear, and Washington Sundar too has ticked the right boxes. With regard to Jasprit Bumrah, clarity is expected before the team links up to commence its preparations.India will play Afghanistan in three T20Is on September 13, 15 and 17. Although the matches are being played in Delhi, Afghanistan are the official hosts of the bilateral series.The Indian team will depart for the Asian Games from Delhi on September 18. Before the start of the Asian Games, Team India will also play a solitary T20I against Japan on September 22 at the Sano International Cricket Ground in Tochigi Prefecture.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pratika Rawal’s India comeback gets another boost as she replaces injured Jemimah for Asian Games
articles.summary: Cricket News: Top-order batter Pratika Rawal has been included in India’s women’s cricket squad for the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as a replacement fo.
articles.body: Top-order batter Pratika Rawal has been included in India’s women’s cricket squad for the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, as a replacement for injured Jemimah Rodrigues.Jemimah continues to recover from a hamstring injury she suffered while playing for Southern Brave in The Hundred on August 3. The injury had already ruled her out of the ongoing Women’s Asia Cup in Dubai and the Asian Games.Rawal gets Asian Games call-upRawal was initially named as Jemimah’s replacement only for the Asia Cup, with no official word at the time on who would take her place in the Asian Games squad. However, a BCCI source confirmed on Wednesday that Rawal’s name was already included in the 15-member squad submitted for the Asian Games, meaning she will travel to Japan as Jemimah’s replacement.The 17-year-old made her T20I debut during the ongoing Asia Cup and has been used at No. 3 by the Indian team management. She has scored 22, 10 and 4 in her three league-stage appearances so far.A long road back for RawalRawal’s return to international cricket came after a lengthy injury layoff. She had not played competitive T20 cricket since November 2024 before her Asia Cup call-up and was also forced to miss the 2026 Women’s Premier League after an ankle injury suffered during the 2025 Women’s ODI World Cup. She had been preparing to join Warwickshire for the One Day Cup in England when the India call came. UP Warriorz had bought her for Rs 50 lakh at the WPL auction last year, but she could not feature in the 2026 season.India head to Japan as defending championsIndia will enter the women’s cricket competition at the Asian Games as defending champions after beating Sri Lanka by 19 runs in the final of the previous edition in Hangzhou. The eight-team competition is scheduled to run from September 17 to 22, with India joined by Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Japan, Thailand, Malaysia and China.India’s Asian Games squad: Harmanpreet Kaur (captain), Smriti Mandhana (vice-captain), Shafali Verma, Pratika Rawal, Bharti Fulmali, Richa Ghosh (WK), G Kamalini (WK), Deepti Sharma, Radha Yadav, Prema Rawat, Arundhati Reddy, Kranti Gaud, Renuka Singh, N Sree Charani and Nandni Sharma.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Emilio Gay: England batter has 'done enough' to retain spot for South Africa tour - Sir Alastair Cook
articles.summary: England batter Emilio Gay has done enough to lock in an opener's spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to Sir Alastair Cook.
articles.body:
England opener Emilio Gay should retain his spot for their winter tour of South Africa, according to former captain Sir Alastair Cook.

Gay made a Test-best 60 from 114 balls to blunt Pakistan's attack which helped England seize control on day one at Edgbaston.

The 26-year-old left-hander's tally of 261 runs, at an average of 26.1, might not look particularly eye-catching.

But in an English summer where ball has dominated bat - Ben Duckett is England's only centurion in six home Tests so far - the Durham left-hander has shown a willingness to grind it out.

Cook, who made almost 12,000 runs as an opener for England, has been impressed with the character the Durham left-hander has shown to make tough runs at the top of the order.

"I think Emilio Gay's played really nicely. I would say he's confident and intense," Cook told Test Match Special.

"He is definitely a run-getter when he gets in. He seems to have that real stubborn and strong will to make it count if he can.

"He has done enough for me to take him to South Africa to continue the progress of a player where the pitches will be slightly easier to bat on and he should open the batting."

According to CricViz, Gay has left or defended 61% of the pace deliveries he's faced since his debut against New Zealand in June.

Dom Sibley in 2020 (68% left or defended) was the last English opener to register a higher percentage in a home summer.

During his innings on Wednesday, Gay left or defended 65 deliveries and Cook "likes how late he defends the ball" with a patient approach to more attacking strokeplay.

Gay scored the first 12 runs of his half-century off 43 balls before his next 38 came off 52 balls.

He hit nine fours and has scored 68% of his Test runs in boundaries - the joint-highest of any England batter with at least 250 runs in the red-ball format.

"If you take Gay's innings, and what I've seen of him, he's not hunting that drive too often. He waits for it to come into there," added Cook.

"He scores off the back foot through the off side as well. He scored through the leg side and timed them through mid-wicket so he does have an all-round game. He's not limited to the off side."

Given Pakistan's flimsy batting - bowled out for 133 in their first innings here - it could end up being Gay's final Test innings of the summer.

With Jacob Bethell set to return for the tour of South Africa following injury, the selection of a top-order batter for the winter is likely to be a scrap between Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Gay for two places.

Only Harry Brook (six occasions) has passed 30 more times than Gay (five) during a challenging summer for batters.

Although Gay has struggled to play back of a length bowling with seven dismissals in the 7-9 metre length range which has highlighted a potential weakness.

Former England captain Michael Vaughan said Gay "played nicely" but might reflect on an missed opportunity to reach three figures for the first time after he dragged on a delivery from Razaullah Khan.

"Emilio Gay found his balance early. He had it hard at the start and then he found his flow," Vaughan said.

"He'll be really disappointed to get out for 60. He'll be desperate to get his first Test match century and I thought it was on today.

"That extra little bit of pace from Razaullah and a little lack of concentration at the end of the day has cost him."

England seamer Josh Tongue said Gay's rigorous preparation has helped him develop the necessary powers of concentration for Test cricket.

"The one thing I've seen in Emilio is he trains really hard in the nets. He'll bat for ages, putting a lot of hard work in, and it's shown on the pitch," added Tongue.

"Even last week at Lord's, he had two quite horrible dismissals, but I felt today he batted unbelievable on a tricky pitch.

"He was obviously really disappointed with how he got out. It's not a nice feeling, chopping on, but he's put the team in a really good position for tomorrow."

articles.title: 'A ball won't kill you, but bullets can': Rashid Khan opens up on his childhood in war-torn Afghanistan
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: From a war-torn nation to making a mark on the world stage, Afghanistan cricket has come a long way. The team has produced stunning perform.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: From a war-torn nation to making a mark on the world stage, Afghanistan cricket has come a long way. The team has produced stunning performances, challenged some of the best sides in the world and pulled off big wins against top teams. Once seen as minnows, Afghanistan have slowly shed that tag and emerged as a team capable of becoming a nightmare for the opposition.As Afghanistan prepare to face India in a three-match T20I series, starting Sunday at the Arun Jaitley Stadium in Delhi, star all-rounder Rashid Khan opened up about the challenges he faced as a child in the war-torn country and how those experiences helped shape his mindset.Rashid is part of the Afghanistan T20I squad for the series against India, with all three matches scheduled to be played in Delhi.During a podcast, with 'The Parenting Pause', Rashid was asked: "You were born into a country which had some level of conflict. There was sort of war. There was some instability. Your memories?"“Well, I think this cricket is just a normal thing, you know. And as I mentioned, what our parents have gone through, when they share their life experience with us, we are, like, you know, so blessed. This is nothing. This pressure is nothing. What we are doing in our life is nothing compared to what they have gone through. You know how it was in Afghanistan 30 years back, 35 years back, and in those days how our parents struggled in the war, like, you know, 40 years back," Rashid said.“My mom and dad, they share their experience — how we went from this place to that place and how hard it was for them to go through all those things. So I was like, they have seen bullets going up in the air. For us to see a ball going up in the air, that is just easy. You know, it won't kill you, but that can kill you. So, to have that kind of mentality — it's just nothing, you just need to go for it — you can do it. You won't die. It's not something that you're going to die from. And you just need to have a strong mindset.Rashid said the mental strength he has developed over the years came largely from watching his parents deal with difficult situations.“And I feel it's all come from my parents. You know, what kind of mindset they had, how strong they were at that particular time, you know, to help and to raise your kids as well in having those kind of tough situations. I think they were the strongest, and I feel like we just got that mentality from our parents.“And whenever facing any tough days, tough time, I just think about how tough that would have been. But they never let themselves down. So why should I let myself down with this pressure?Rashid said remembering what his parents went through helps him put pressure and difficult moments into perspective.“So I think it just all comes mentally, like, you know, to have those things in the mind, and then you become mentally stronger. So yeah, I think I feel I keep that with myself, and it just helps me in a tougher time. It just helps me, and everything just goes in seconds when I think about it. You put everything in perspective. Yeah. So nothing remains.“It's just like, okay, there is a saying now, and they say that what doesn't kill you only makes you stronger.”Rashid believes difficult situations can also become opportunities to learn and grow."It only teaches you and makes you stronger and gives you a better listener. So I think in a pressure situation, tough situation, you know, I'm so happy for that time because it's not only the pressure situation, it's just the best time for me to learn and to get the good experience and to become a better person, physically and mentally," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1936, an Indian fast bowler's delivery killed a bird at Lord's. The bird was stuffed and mounted on the same ball and now sits in the MCC Museum
articles.summary: Cricket News: Every corner of Lord's Cricket Ground has a story. Since opening in 1814, the venue in London's St John's Wood has become one of cricket's most iconic.
articles.body: Every corner of Lord's Cricket Ground has a story. Since opening in 1814, the venue in London's St John's Wood has become one of cricket's most iconic grounds. Generations of cricketers have played here, and many of the game's most memorable moments have unfolded on its field.Away from the pitch, Lord's is also home to one of cricket's biggest collections of history. Inside the ground sits the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) Museum, which was inaugurated in 1953 by HRH, The Duke of Edinburgh. It is one of the oldest sporting museums in the world and houses some of the game's most famous artefacts.Visitors can see Kapil Dev's 1983 World Cup-winning memorabilia, the Ashes urn, bats used by WG Grace, and many other pieces of history from different eras of cricket. But among all those exhibits, one display continues to stand out for its unusual story — a cricket ball mounted with a stuffed sparrow.The day a cricket ball hit a sparrowThe incident happened on July 3, 1936, during a match between Cambridge University and the MCC at Lord's.Indian fast bowler Jahangir Khan was representing Cambridge University. He was bowling to Tom Pearce when one of his deliveries struck a sparrow in mid-air. The bird died instantly after being hit by the ball.What made the incident even stranger was what happened next. Pearce still managed to play the delivery, and the sparrow fell near the stumps.As recorded by Wisden Almanack: "TN Pearce, the batsman, managed to play the ball and the bird fell against the stumps without dislodging a bail."The unusual moment immediately became part of cricket folklore., and instead of discarding the bird, it was preserved.How the sparrow became a museum exhibitThe sparrow was stuffed and mounted on the very cricket ball that hit it.The display was later placed in the Memorial Gallery at Lord's and has remained one of the museum's most recognised exhibits ever since.The museum describes it as one of its "best-loved artefacts"."The unfortunate bird was stuffed and mounted upon the ball that killed it and subsequently displayed in the Memorial Gallery at Lord's. It has since become one of the most curious and best-loved artefacts ever displayed at the Ground."For decades, thousands of visitors have stopped to look at the sparrow and the ball, making it one of the museum's most talked-about exhibits despite having nothing to do with a famous innings or a major trophy.What scientists discovered 84 years laterThe sparrow remained on display at Lord's for decades before experts carried out conservation work in 2020.It was sent to London's Natural History Museum, where specialists examined and restored it.The conservation work revealed something that had not been known since 1936. The bird was identified as a young adult male sparrow.The museum also repaired damage that had appeared over time. According to the MCC Museum, "Conservation work at the Natural History Museum in early 2020 revealed for the first time that the sparrow had been a young adult male."The restoration included repairs to skin splits across the abdomen, a loose wing, and cleaning away dust and dirt collected over many years inside the museum.The work was carried out to ensure the exhibit could continue to be displayed for future visitors.The bird has left Lord's only twiceThe conservation trip in 2020 was only the second time the sparrow had left Lord's since becoming part of the museum.Its first trip came in 2006, when it travelled to the Netherlands.The sparrow became part of the Grand House Sparrow exhibition at the Natural History Museum of Rotterdam, where it was displayed. After returning to Lord's, it continued to occupy its place inside the MCC Museum.The museum noted that the conservation work in London should help preserve the exhibit for years to come."Its more recent trip should guarantee that it remains fit to delight visitors to the MCC Museum for many years to come."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Just grab the piece of wood': Rashid Khan recalls growing up without a proper bat
articles.summary: Cricket News: Rashid Khan has become the most recognised figure in Afghanistan cricket and the country’s first global cricket superstar. He now has franchise contra.
articles.body: Rashid Khan has become the most recognised figure in Afghanistan cricket and the country’s first global cricket superstar. He now has franchise contracts worth millions of dollars and plays leagues around the world. He also has access to world-class cricket facilities. But his journey began without even the basic equipment needed to practise.Rashid is not a big turner of the ball. Instead, he puts batters under pressure with his speed through the air, like his bowling idol Shahid Afridi, while keeping a stump-to-stump line. His main weapon is an accurate googly, while he has several variations. As a batter, Rashid can clear the boundary late in an innings and has helped turn modest totals into match-winning ones for his teams.However, he did not always have a proper bat to practise with. "For us (Rashid and his brothers) it was very hard to to buy the bat at that particular time. "What we used to do is just to grab the piece of wood and then trying to make the handle of that like you know by cutting it. That's how our cricket bat was like, you know, it wasn't like a proper bat," Rashid Khan recently said in a podcast with 'The Parenting Pause' YouTube channel.He also said he had no access to formal cricket coaching for a long time and learned the game from his brothers. "I learned the game by just watching my brothers play at home. They're playing cricket and you're watching them and then you're saying, 'Okay, that's how you hold the bat. That's how you play the shot,'" the Afghanistan leg-spinner added."I used to just field for them and I was very good in fielding. After a while, I started getting opportunity to bat a little bit and to bowl as well."Rashid said he learned leg-spin because all his brothers were leg-spinners. "My brothers, they were all leg spinners as well. They could bowl leg spin and and that's how I understood that okay I want to bowl like that."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Masked protesters mistake Pakistan U-19 cricket team for asylum seekers in Portsmouth
articles.summary: Cricket News: A group of masked protesters gathered outside a four-star hotel in Portsmouth after wrongly believing that a group of asylum seekers had been taken th.
articles.body: A group of masked protesters gathered outside a four-star hotel in Portsmouth after wrongly believing that a group of asylum seekers had been taken there. They later discovered that the people staying at the hotel were members of Pakistan's Under-19 cricket team.Around 40 people gathered outside the Marriott hotel on Tuesday evening, with many wearing balaclavas or other face coverings. The protesters had reportedly seen a group of men they believed were asylum seekers arriving at the hotel.George Madgwick, a Reform councillor whose ward includes the hotel, was called to the scene to help resolve the situation. He spoke to the hotel manager, who explained that the men were Pakistan's Under-19 cricketers, who are in England for a tour and are using the Marriott as their base.Madgwick also spoke to the team's coach and was shown proof that the group were cricketers."I went out to the protesters and told them, 'You've got it wrong guys, it's a cricket club.' They left within a couple of minutes. It was a massively unfortunate incident," Madgwick told The Guardian.He said the misunderstanding was partly because the coach carrying the players was operated by the same company that had transported asylum seekers who recently arrived in Portsmouth by boat."From the perspective of the people of Portsmouth who are already on high alert, this was a coach from the same company which was turning up with about 40 foreign men," Madgwick said.The incident came after tensions rose in Portsmouth following the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats from France. Hundreds of people, many wearing balaclavas, clashed with police in the city on Sunday evening. Police are investigating possible assaults and criminal damage.A day earlier, crowds dressed in black and wearing balaclavas had blocked a road near the port of Dover. Far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who is closely linked to Tommy Robinson, said he had organised both demonstrations.Madgwick said he understood the concerns of local residents but acknowledged that the incident was far from ideal."It doesn't make our city look like the welcoming city it is. But it's reflective of the climate we live in, and where people are deeply concerned about the issues," he said.Madgwick had earlier posted on Facebook asking people not to go to the hotel after residents contacted him about what they believed were migrants staying there. He later made the post private after it attracted abusive comments.The England and Wales Cricket Board has since contacted the Pakistan Cricket Board to check on the wellbeing of the players and is reviewing security arrangements for the remainder of the team's tour.Pakistan Under-19 recently played England Under-19 in a four-day Test, losing by 10 runs. The teams are scheduled to meet in a one-day match at Arundel on Wednesday, before another ODI in Guildford on Saturday.Pakistan's senior men's team is also currently in England for the third and final Test against England at Edgbaston.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Varun Chakravarthy's second act: Why India's mystery spinner still believes he's only halfway through his career
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: For a cricketer who made his international debut at 29, Varun Chakravarthy measures time differently.Now, at 35, he has just lived through .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For a cricketer who made his international debut at 29, Varun Chakravarthy measures time differently.Now, at 35, he has just lived through a rollercoaster year: a T20 World Cup title on home soil where he finished as India's joint-highest wicket-taker with 14 wickets, an IPL campaign played through hairline fractures in his left hand and toe, and then the first muscle injury of his career that forced him into weeks of rehabilitation.Yet, ask him where he stands in his journey, and his answer is strikingly uncomplicated."At this stage of my career, I still feel I'm in my first half of my career because I started cricket very late. So I still feel there's a long way to go," Chakaravarthy said in an interaction with TimesofIndia.com, facilitated by equipment manufacturer ASICS.It is an outlook that perhaps explains Chakravarthy's unconventional rise better than any statistic. The Tamil Nadu spinner has never been one for grand declarations or five-year plans. In a sport as volatile as T20 cricket, he prefers chasing the next small improvement rather than the next milestone.Now fully recovered from the Grade 2 left hamstring injury he suffered during the England T20I series, Chakravarthy returns just in time for a busy stretch: three T20Is against Afghanistan, a historic one-off international against Japan, and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, where defending champions India begin directly from the quarterfinals.Learning a new kind of injuryUntil this summer, pain had always arrived the same way for Chakravarthy, through collisions, impact or bad luck.A torn muscle was unfamiliar territory."This is actually my first ever muscle injury. So all of my injuries have been impact injuries and other accidents that have happened on field. The expertise at CoE helped me and people helped me to gain my confidence. Every person working there helped me," he explained.Recovery meant long days at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, where rebuilding confidence became as important as rebuilding strength. The rehabilitation, too, was relentless."Definitely, I spent a lot of time there and did a lot of running and did a lot of strength training, which helped me."For a bowler whose craft depends on rhythm as much as deception, returning isn't simply about being medically fit. It's about trusting the body enough to express the imagination that makes him so difficult to read."Yeah, it will take some time to gain confidence. But once you gain confidence, you just start becoming more expressive and that's how it is," reasoned the 35-year-old.Rather than treating injury lay-offs as wasted time, Chakravarthy sees them as opportunities to work on parts of the game that competition rarely allows."When you're away, you can start sharpening your skills. You can upskill yourself, which you don't get much time to do when you're playing continuously."Why shoes matter more than mysteryMystery spin is often associated with wrists, fingers and release points. Chakravarthy begins somewhere else entirely: the feet.His partnership with ASICS may be commercial, but his relationship with the brand predates the endorsement. He says he had already switched to their shoes around 2022 before formally signing a deal in January 2026.More revealing is how clinically he breaks down footwear."For a bowler, shoes are the biggest equipment they can have. Batters, they have many other equipments, but for a bowler, it's the shoes only," said Varun."As a spinner, your feet start becoming little broader as in it starts changing shape once you pivot because the spinners have to pivot more after landing. So broad shoes in the toe area that is very important," he added.Add a supportive heel counter and lighter weight, he says, and you've got the essentials of a spinner's toolkit.It's the kind of detail that reflects Chakravarthy's evolution from architect to elite cricketer: analytical, process-driven and constantly searching for marginal gains.The curiosity beyond cricketThe Asian Games, which begin on September 19, offer something even ICC events cannot — a sporting village shared with athletes from dozens of disciplines. For Chakravarthy, that might be the biggest attraction."It's my first time in Japan. I've never been to Japan and any games also. So all I've played is ICC tournaments and ACC tournaments," said Chakravarthy, his excitement quite evident in his voice."I'm very much looking forward to meeting other athletes also from other different sports and all those things.""I want to see how a 100-metre athlete prepares himself, how a badminton professional prepares himself or herself," he went on to state.In India's increasingly packed cricket calendar, opportunities for cross-pollination are rare. The Asian Games provide a window into sporting cultures that cricketers seldom experience.That openness may also prove useful on the field. The pitches at Korogi Sports Park are expected to differ from familiar Indian surfaces, and Chakravarthy believes adaptability will define the bowling attack's success more than preconceived plansGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'I knew we'd lose 3-0': Wasim Akram tears into Pakistan cricket setup
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan great Wasim Akram believes the crisis engulfing the country's cricket system has become so deep-rooted that even he cannot fix it on his own,.
articles.body: Pakistan great Wasim Akram believes the crisis engulfing the country's cricket system has become so deep-rooted that even he cannot fix it on his own, pointing to problems that extend from the national team to the domestic structure.The former Pakistan captain said the team's struggles cannot be blamed on a single person or department, with shortcomings evident in batting, bowling and fielding as well as instability in first-class cricket.Akram said he had expected Pakistan to struggle badly in their ongoing Test series in England because of the weaknesses within the side."I knew before the Test series started in England we would lose three nil because of the glaring problems in our batting and bowling," he said.Pakistan's problems were again exposed on the opening day of the third Test. After seven players from the original squad were released, the visitors were forced into four changes and fielded three debutants.They were asked to bat first on an overcast day and quickly found themselves in trouble. Pakistan lost their first four wickets inside the opening hour, with three more falling before lunch, before the innings ended at just 133 in the 34th over.The top five batters all fell for single-digit scores. Saud Shakeel offered some resistance with a positive 43, while Abbas was Pakistan's second-highest scorer with 21.England's Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer picked up three wickets each, accounting for Pakistan's top four, while Josh Tongue continued his impressive form by claiming four wickets.Akram, however, believes the problems go well beyond what is happening in the current Test series.The legendary fast bowler said he is regularly asked whether he can step in and help Pakistan cricket, but argued that the scale of the problems makes it impossible for one individual to provide a solution."I get asked all the time, 'Can you do something to help Pakistan cricket?' But the issues are a lot deeper. These are the top players, there's nothing else there. The systems aren't there below that," he said.Akram particularly highlighted the lack of consistency and patience in Pakistan's domestic cricket structure. He believes constant changes and instability at first-class level have contributed to the failure to develop enough quality players for the national team.He also criticised the Pakistan Cricket Board's inconsistent decision-making, saying the problems have built up across the entire cricket ecosystem rather than being restricted to selection calls, coaches or dressing-room decisions."Our batting is struggling, our bowling is below average, and our fielding is worse. It's not rocket science," Akram said.According to the former fast bowler, Pakistan's current performances are therefore a reflection of wider structural issues. He stressed that responsibility for the team's decline rests with multiple stakeholders and cannot simply be placed on the players or coaching staff.For Akram, the immediate problems are visible in England, but fixing Pakistan cricket will require greater stability and patience much further down the system.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Harshit Rana, Nitish Reddy doubtful for Afghanistan series; Jasprit Bumrah call on Thursday
articles.summary: Cricket News: New Delhi: There are doubts over the fitness status of Harshit Rana and Nitish Kumar Reddy, with both unlikely to join the Indian team for the T20 ser.
articles.body: New Delhi: There are doubts over the fitness status of Harshit Rana and Nitish Kumar Reddy, with both unlikely to join the Indian team for the T20 series against Afghanistan in Delhi, TOI has learnt. Rana and Reddy, along with recovering star fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah, underwent match simulation tests at the Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru on Wednesday. While Rana is all but ruled out, Reddy might still play a few games.The India T20I team is scheduled to start training at the Arun Jaitley Stadium from Thursday for the T20I series.“CoE wants to take a cautious approach before clearing the players. The players are clinically fit but they may require another 10-15 days to be match fit,” BCCI sources said, adding, “Selectors will have a discussion with CoE and team management about the situation on Thursday morning. Bumrah’s participation in the series and the Asian Games will also be discussed.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tilak Varma’s Duleep Trophy dream run ends at 99, but Test goal remains
articles.summary: Cricket News: Chennai: Tilak Varma was finally dismissed in this year’s Duleep Trophy, falling agonisingly short of a second century. Despite being dismissed for 99.
articles.body: Chennai: Tilak Varma was finally dismissed in this year’s Duleep Trophy, falling agonisingly short of a second century. Despite being dismissed for 99, the South Zone captain’s red-ball ambitions stay intact, even though his team is staring at a big loss against East at the MA Chidambaram Stadium.Tilak, who had scored a century and a half-century in South Zone’s semifinal win against North Zone without being dismissed, battled through the Chennai heat on Wednesday against a quality East Zone attack. He was the last man to fall, giving a return catch to off-spinner Kounain Quraishi, as South were eventually bowled out for 336, conceding a massive 372-run first-innings lead.East, opting to bat again rather than send their bowlers back out, were 212-5 at stumps on Day Four, stretching their lead to 584.For Tilak, however, the larger picture remained clear. The 23-year-old left-hander has made no secret about his desire to play Test cricket for India.“I always say to everyone that I want to play red-ball cricket for India, that’s my biggest goal. As a kid, I thought I would play Test cricket first and then white-ball cricket. Red-ball cricket has always been my favourite, it’s my ‘A’ game,” Tilak said.“Over the last five-six years, I have played a lot of white-ball cricket and become good at it. Red-ball cricket is still my favourite, but I am comfortable with both now,” said Tilak.Tilak resumed the day on 56 and immediately took the attack to Mohammed Shami (2-42), striking two boundaries in the opening over. He and Chama Milind took 44 runs from the nine overs of Shami and Mukesh Kumar’s (3-62) combined first spell, putting them under pressure.Shami conceded 25 in his first four overs after giving away only 17 in 11 overs on Day 3.Kishan breaks 16-year-old recordEast’s second innings saw Ishan Kishan continue his first-innings form with 80 off 98 balls, while Shikhar Mohan (52) also remained among the runs.Ishan Kishan amassed 350 runs across both innings of the Duleep Trophy final, surpassing Dinesh Karthik’s aggregate of 333 runs from the 2010 final to set a new record for the most runs in the tournament final.Brief scores: East Zone 708 & 212-5 (I Kishan 80, S Mohan 52; Md Siraj 1-17) vs South Zone 336 (T Varma 99; M Kumar 3-62, Md Shami 2-42, M Quraishi 2-99).Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India vs Bangladesh: Harmanpreet Kaur’s side eyes Asia Cup final after dominant run
articles.summary: Cricket News: Seven-time champions India will start as overwhelming favourites against a gritty Bangladesh in the first semifinal of the 2026 Women’s Asia Cup at th.
articles.body: Seven-time champions India will start as overwhelming favourites against a gritty Bangladesh in the first semifinal of the 2026 Women’s Asia Cup at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Thursday.Beyond the on-field contest, India-Bangladesh cricket ties continue to carry a political backdrop. Ever since the regime change in Bangladesh a couple of years ago, relations between New Delhi and Dhaka have been strained.The impact has spilled into cricket. The BCCI withdrew Bangladesh left-arm pacer Mustafizur Rahman, signed by Kolkata Knight Riders, from IPL 2026. Bangladesh subsequently pulled out of the 2026 men’s T20 World Cup in India, while India’s white-ball tour of Bangladesh has been postponed repeatedly amid the political tensions.India have been the standout side of the tournament, topping Group A with three wins from three matches. Harmanpreet Kaur’s side will be keen to reclaim the continental crown after losing last year’s final to Sri Lanka in Colombo.The biggest highlight of India’s campaign has been vice-captain Smriti Mandhana’s blazing 124 off 64 balls against Hong Kong. During that knock, she surpassed former skipper Mithali Raj to become the leading run-scorer in women’s international cricket across formats. India’s spinners also dismantled Pakistan for just 55 before sealing a seven-wicket win inside nine overs. Alongside Mandhana, Shafali Verma has continued her explosive form.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Hardik Pandya set for India ‘A’ stint before India return
articles.summary: Cricket News: Mumbai: Senior all-rounder Hardik Pandya has been named in the India ‘A’ squad for the three-match one-day series against Australia ‘A’ in Puducherry .
articles.body: Mumbai: Senior all-rounder Hardik Pandya has been named in the India ‘A’ squad for the three-match one-day series against Australia ‘A’ in Puducherry in October, subject to regaining full fitness, the BCCI announced on Wednesday. The move means Pandya will also miss India’s three-match ODI series against West Indies, beginning on September 27.Pandya, sidelined since the end of IPL 2026 because of a quadricep injury followed by a shin problem, which saw him miss the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan starting in New Delhi from September 13, has been undergoing rehabilitation at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru.Sources told TOI that the 32-year-old has resumed bowling, averaging seven overs daily, and is expected to be fully fit by September 21-22. However, the selectors appear keen to assess Pandya’s match readiness at India ‘A’ level before considering him for the senior side.With an ODI World Cup scheduled for October-November 2027, the team management wants him bowling a full quota of 10 overs regularly.Ind ‘A’ multi-day squad: Devdutt Padikkal (C), Sai Sudharsan (VC), Aman Mokhade, Ayush Pandey, Yash Rathod, Shaik Rasheed, Kumar Kushagra (WK), Shams Mulani, Tanush Kotian, Tushar Deshpande, Anshul Kamboj, Praful Hinge, N Jagadeesan (WK), Nachiket Bhute, V Vyshak.Ind ‘A’ one-day squad: Ruturaj Gaikwad (C), Devdutt Padikkal (VC), P Arya, S Sudharsan, Rajat Patidar, Kumar Kushagra (WK), Nishant Sindhu, Vipraj Nigam, Arshin Kulkarni, Arshad Khan, Naman Dhir, Hardik Pandya, Prabhsimran Singh (WK), Gurjapneet Singh, Yash Thakur.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'We’re not used to facing that': Pakistan hide behind 'conditions' as batting woes continue in England
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan’s batting problems continued in the third and final Test against England as the visitors were bowled out for 133 at Edgbaston on the first da.
articles.body: Pakistan’s batting problems continued in the third and final Test against England as the visitors were bowled out for 133 at Edgbaston on the first day. After losing the first two Tests at Leeds and Lord’s, Pakistan made several changes to their squad but could not stop another batting collapse.England captain Joe Root won the toss and elected to bowl. Josh Tongue took 4-42, while Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer picked up three wickets each as Pakistan were dismissed in 44.3 overs.Saud Shakeel was Pakistan’s top scorer with 43, but the rest of the batting order again failed to spend time at the crease. This was the fifth time Pakistan had batted in the series and, on each occasion, they have been bowled out for less than 200.England then moved to 156-4 by stumps, taking a 23-run lead. Emilio Gay and Harry Brook scored fifties to put the hosts in control before the close of play. Joe Root was dismissed lbw, the 10th time he has been out that way in his last 13 innings.Shakeel said Pakistan were making the same mistakes with the bat and had failed to deal with the conditions."It's depressing, we're making the same mistake as a batting unit," Shakeel said. "We're getting out in bunches and there were lots of soft dismissals today. We're trying, but yes it's frustrating that we keep making the same mistakes. I don't think it's a confidence issue. If you don't have the confidence to play at this level, then you don't deserve to play here. But in difficult conditions, poor form can be quite hard to break out of."He said the team was working to address its problems but had found it difficult to handle the movement offered to England's bowlers.“We’re working hard, it’s not like we aren’t trying,” Shakeel said. “There’s a lot of lateral movement and we’re not used to facing that, but we are trying our best. I’m not saying our batting group has not struggled, we have accepted that. But the conditions have been difficult.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Unbelievable stat! Shubman Gill did it alone, Pakistan still can't do it as a team
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan's batting crisis has reached an extraordinary point in their ongoing Test series against England. After three Tests, the entire Pakistan team.
articles.body: Pakistan's batting crisis has reached an extraordinary point in their ongoing Test series against England. After three Tests, the entire Pakistan team is now just 11 runs short of the 754 runs Shubman Gill scored on his own during India's five-Test series in England last year.Gill finished India's five-Test campaign with 754 runs, establishing himself as one of the standout performers of the series. Pakistan, meanwhile, have managed 743 runs across the first two Tests and the opening innings of the third Test at Edgbaston.Their latest collapse, when they were bowled out for just 133 on Wednesday, has left Pakistan tantalisingly close to an unwanted statistical milestone.Pakistan's batting crisis deepensThe latest failure came at a particularly turbulent time for Pakistan cricket. Following defeats at Headingley and Lord's, the Pakistan Cricket Board made sweeping changes to the Test setup. Seven players were removed from the squad, while the coaching staff was also sacked as the board attempted to shake up a side that had struggled badly during the series.Yet the changes failed to produce an immediate response at Edgbaston.Asked at the toss how difficult it had been to lead Pakistan through such turbulent circumstances, Babar Azam insisted the situation had not affected him."Not difficult. Yes, after that we had a couple of changes, but I think a good opportunity to new boys, and yes we are trying to do our best in this match," Babar said.The first session, however, suggested that Pakistan's problems had travelled with them to Birmingham.Another top-order collapsePut into bat, Pakistan lost wickets regularly and were bowled out for 133.Ollie Robinson struck first, trapping recalled opener Saim Ayub lbw for a duck to claim his 100th Test wicket. Jofra Archer then accounted for debutant Azan Awais before Abdullah Shafique fell to Robinson.Shan Masood was next, caught at mid-wicket off Archer after another poor cross-bat stroke.Tongue then took over, dismissing Pakistan captain Babar Azam before removing debutants Ghazi Ghori and Imran Randhawa before lunch.Razaullah Khan fell for 11 in the afternoon session, leaving Saud Shakeel as Pakistan's only meaningful resistance.Shakeel, who had made a fighting 97 in the defeat at Lord's, top-scored again with 43 before Tongue bowled him with a sharp inswinging delivery.Archer finished with 3-25, Robinson took 3-15 from 11 overs and Tongue claimed 4-42 as Pakistan were dismissed for 133.England then extended their advantage in the first innings. Ben Duckett was dismissed for 11 by Mohammad Ali, while Jordan Cox fell for four to Mohammad Abbas. But Emilio Gay and Harry Brook both made fifties to put England in command.The hosts reached 156-4 by stumps, taking a 23-run lead despite Joe Root falling lbw for the 10th time in 13 innings.Robinson was particularly impressive, conceding just 15 runs in 11 overs as he moved from 99 to 102 Test wickets. His Test bowling average of 19.1 is the best among post-war bowlers with more than 100 dismissals.Pakistan's 743 runs across the first three Tests so far make the Gill comparison impossible to ignore. Gill scored 754 runs by himself during India's five-Test series in England last year. Pakistan have needed two complete Tests and one innings of a third to get within 11 runs of that tally. The comparison is a striking illustration of the gulf between individual consistency and Pakistan's collective batting output during this series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
